newsitem.title: ZAMBIA: Zambia's Chiluba sees landslide win, turnout low.
newsitem.headline: Zambia's Chiluba sees landslide win, turnout low.

text.p: Zambian President Frederick Chiluba headed on Wednesday for a landslide victory in the southern African country's disputed election which was marked by an opposition boycott and a low turnout.
Chiluba had secured 76 percent of votes cast in 87 of 150 constituencies which had so far reported final results, according to figures released by the elections office.

Chiluba was leading with 600,965 of the 786,583 votes counted by mid-afternoon -- enough to give him at least 50 percent of the estimated 1.1 million votes cast overall, even before results from 63 remaining constituencies were counted.
Election monitors based their forecast of the total turnout on the number of voters who both registered and collected their voting cards, signalling intention to vote.

Political analysts and opposition figures said that while Chiluba was sure of re-election, his victory would be marred by the low turnout, which was partly due to the opposition's call to supporters to boycott the entire election.
Chiluba's closest rival, Zambia Democratic Congress leader Dean Mungomba, polled only 94,237 votes by mid-afternoon.
Seven opposition parties boycotted the poll, charging that Chiluba had rigged the campaign in advance and said they would not recognise the result.
Half of Zambia's 4.6 million eligible voters were excluded from the rolls because of flawed registration.

Former president Kenneth Kaunda, who ruled from independence in 1964 until Chiluba trounced him in Zambia's first free polls in 1991, was barred from contesting the poll by a new law because his parents, from Malawi, were not Zambian.
Kaunda led the opposition boycott of the campaign and called for economic sanctions on Zambia.
Chiluba last week rejected a public call from South African President Nelson Mandela to delay the election.

The Committee for a Clean Campaign, a Zambian umbrella group of 19 non-governmental and civic organisations which monitored the ballot, said that while the voting itself had been correct, the run-up to the elections was designed to give the ruling party an unfair advantage.
The committee said that flawed voter registration, abuses of government resources and partisan state-run media had favoured Chiluba's Movement for Multi-party Democracy (MMD).
"In view of all this, the 1996 presidential and parliamentary elections cannot be said to have been free and fair," the statement said.
An international observer group, however, said the election was "generally free and fair".
"The process was good and transparent, and we have not detected any evidence of foul play," said a statement by the monitoring group, working under the auspices of the Christian Council of Zambia.

"We did not see any evidence of rigging or intimidation," the international group added. It included monitors from a number of southern African states plus Canada, Denmark, Sweden, Australia and Germany.
Counting officials expected to have the final tally by late Wednesday.
